bill.title: Nuclear Family Priority Act
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: Immigration law firms would see changes in demand for services related to family-based visa petitions and the new nonimmigrant parent visa category.
Reduced family immigration could affect demand for travel and lodging services related to family visits and relocation.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would sharply reduce the number of family-based immigration visas available each year, lowering the annual cap from 480,000 to 88,000. It would eliminate visa categories for siblings and married children of U.S. citizens, and would remove parents of citizens from the immediate-relative category that currently has no numerical limit. Parents of citizens would instead be eligible for a temporary visa that does not allow them to work or receive public benefits.

plain.whoItTouches: People applying to live here, and their families here.

bill.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act
bill.latestActionText: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 59.

industries.rationale: The bill directly imposes new content-moderation obligations and 48-hour removal requirements on platforms that host user-generated content.
Online publishers and digital media platforms may face compliance obligations if they host user-generated intimate content.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would make it a federal crime to publish intimate images or videos of someone online without their consent, including computer-generated deepfakes, when the publication is intended to cause harm or involves a minor. It would require websites and apps that host user-generated content to remove such images within 48 hours of being notified by the person depicted. Violators would face criminal penalties including prison time, fines, and mandatory restitution to victims.

plain.whoItTouches: Children, and the adults responsible for them. Anyone who uses the internet.

bill.title: No Taxpayer Funding for Abortion and Abortion Insurance Full Disclosure Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committees on the Judiciary, and Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

industries.rationale: The bill directly restricts what health insurance plans may cover and how federal subsidies interact with abortion coverage in qualified health plans.
The bill prohibits federal health care facilities and federal employees from providing abortion services, affecting facilities that currently receive federal funds.
Organizations focused on reproductive health policy and abortion access or restrictions have a direct stake in the regulatory framework this bill establishes.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would make permanent the restrictions on federal funding for abortion services and health insurance coverage that includes abortion. Currently, these restrictions are renewed each year through appropriations bills; the bill would apply them across all federal programs and funds. It would also prohibit qualified health plans offered through insurance marketplaces from covering abortion. The bill includes exceptions for cases of rape, incest, or when the pregnant person's life is in danger.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who buys health insurance. Anyone who pays a medical bill.

bill.title: SAVE Moms and Babies Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
subjects: Drug safety, medical device, and laboratory regulation

industries.rationale: The bill directly prohibits approval of new abortion drugs and imposes significant new regulatory restrictions on already-approved drugs in this category.
The bill creates new certification requirements for prescribing practitioners and mandates they have surgical intervention capability, changing practice obligations.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would prohibit the FDA from approving any new drugs intended to terminate pregnancy. For drugs already approved for this purpose, it would impose new restrictions: requiring in-person dispensing by a specially certified practitioner, prohibiting use after 70 days of gestation, and mandating that the practitioner be able to provide surgical intervention. The bill would also prevent practitioners from both prescribing and dispensing these medications.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who fills a prescription. Anyone who takes a medicine.

bill.title: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
bill.latestActionText: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 466.
subjects: Department of Health and Human Services

industries.rationale: The bill directly funds research grants and regulatory pathways for development of drugs and therapies targeting ALS and neurodegenerative diseases.
Providers treating ALS patients may see changes in available investigational therapies and clinical trial access, though the bill focuses primarily on research and regulatory processes.

bill.plainSummary: This bill extends funding through fiscal year 2031 for federal programs that support research and development of treatments for ALS (Lou Gehrig's disease) and similar neurodegenerative diseases. It requires the National Institutes of Health to track safety data on experimental drugs and mandates that the Food and Drug Administration publish a five-year plan describing how it will help develop and approve therapies for these rare diseases. The bill also continues a public-private partnership between federal agencies and outside organizations working on neurodegenerative disease treatments.

plain.whoItTouches: People with an illness that is still being studied. Anyone who uses the internet.

bill.title: Concerning the National Collegiate Athletic Association policy for eligibility in women's sports.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

industries.rationale: The resolution directly addresses NCAA policy, which governs collegiate athletics at member universities and affects their compliance obligations and program administration.
Changes to NCAA eligibility rules could affect the composition and marketability of collegiate sports programming and events.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution calls on the National Collegiate Athletic Association to withdraw its current policy allowing transgender student-athletes to compete and instead adopt rules requiring participation in women's sports to be based on biological sex. The measure urges the NCAA to mandate that all member conferences implement such a policy across every sport and division. As a resolution, it expresses the position of the House but does not create enforceable law.
